lead: Every pulse that enters a fiber comes out weaker and wider. This unit measures both effects: attenuation in dB per kilometre, split into absorption, scattering and bending, and dispersion in ps per nanometre-kilometre, split into intermodal, chromatic and polarization terms. After it you can compute a link's loss and pulse spread, name the mechanism behind each, and choose the fiber that fixes it.
about: The unit starts with the language of loss: attenuation in dB per kilometre, dBm and the transmission windows. The next three chapters split that one number into absorption, scattering and bending, so you can say which mechanism dominates at which wavelength. The unit then turns to the second kind of degradation, pulse spreading: intermodal dispersion in multimode fiber, chromatic dispersion (material plus waveguide) in single-mode fiber, polarization mode dispersion, and the fibers built to shift or cancel dispersion. It closes with the high-power effects, stimulated Brillouin and Raman scattering, that set a ceiling on the power a fiber can carry.

chapters.idea: Attenuation is the loss of optical power along the fiber, quoted as a coefficient in dB per kilometre, and it decides how far a link can reach before the receiver needs a booster.
chapters.depth: Define the attenuation coefficient α = (10/L) log₁₀(P_in/P_out) in dB/km, where L is the fiber length in km and P_in, P_out are input and output powers in the same unit. Total loss in dB is A = αL, so losses add in dB while powers multiply. Explain the decibel with two anchor points: 3 dB halves the power, 10 dB is a factor of ten. List the four loss families — absorption (2.2), scattering (2.3), bending (2.4) and joint and connector loss (Unit 3) — and stress that dB values simply add. Give the standard window figures of about 2.5 dB/km at 850 nm, 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm and 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, plus the water peak near 1380 nm in older fiber. Mention that 1 dB = 0.2303 nepers, since some syllabi state α in nepers per metre. Say why long-haul links live at 1550 nm.

figure.aria: A curve of fiber attenuation against wavelength, high near 850 nm, low at 1310 nm and 1550 nm, with a small bump at the 1380 nm water peak.

chapters.example: A 1550 nm link uses fiber with α = 0.2 dB/km and launches 1 mW. (a) Find the loss over 80 km. (b) Find the power arriving at the far end. (c) Find the maximum length before the power falls to 1 µW. Answer: (a) A = 0.2 × 80 = 16 dB. (b) P_out = 1 mW × 10^(−16/10) = 1 mW × 10^(−1.6) = 0.0251 mW ≈ 25 µW. (c) The allowed loss is 10 log₁₀(1 mW / 1 µW) = 30 dB, so L = 30 / 0.2 = 150 km.
chapters.trap: Writing the loss as α / L instead of α L, and mixing dB with dB/km. A second trap is adding powers in mW and then converting, instead of adding the losses in dB.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the ray picture, total internal reflection and the meaning of guided power.
chapters.leave: Power budget arithmetic, rise-time budget and how attenuation is actually measured belong to Unit 5. The individual loss mechanisms are chapters 2 to 4.

chapters.idea: Silica glass itself absorbs in the ultraviolet and the infrared, and impurities such as OH⁻ and metal ions absorb at specific wavelengths; together they set part of the loss floor of a fiber.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the tail physics in detail. Intrinsic absorption has two parts. The ultraviolet tail comes from electrons of the SiO₂ network being excited across the band gap, and it falls steeply as wavelength rises. The infrared tail comes from Si–O bond vibrations and multiphonon absorption, rising steeply beyond about 1.6 µm. Between the two tails silica is transparent from roughly 0.4 to 1.6 µm. Extrinsic absorption comes from impurities: the OH⁻ ion, whose fundamental vibration sits near 2.73 µm with overtones near 1.38, 0.95 and 0.72 µm, and transition metal ions such as Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Cr³⁺ and Ni²⁺ with broad bands. Modern processing has pushed metal absorption below 0.01 dB/km, so only the OH⁻ overtones matter. Some syllabi call intrinsic absorption 'fundamental' and extrinsic absorption 'impurity' absorption.

figure.aria: A tree splitting absorption into intrinsic silica tails and extrinsic impurity bands, with the OH⁻ overtone marked as the one that still matters.

chapters.example: An old fiber has an extra 0.4 dB/km from the OH⁻ overtone at 1380 nm. A 25 km link runs at 1380 nm with a total of 0.75 dB/km, of which 0.35 dB/km is Rayleigh scattering. (a) Find the extra loss in dB caused by the OH⁻ ion over the link. (b) Find the fraction of launched power lost to it. Answer: (a) 0.4 × 25 = 10 dB. (b) The power ratio is 10^(−10/10) = 0.1, so 90% of the launched power is lost to the water peak.
chapters.trap: Placing the water peak at 1550 nm, or treating the whole 1300–1500 nm range as unusable. The other trap is calling an impurity effect intrinsic.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for the attenuation coefficient, and Unit 1 for the picture of silica glass.
chapters.leave: Scattering and bending losses are 2.3 and 2.4. Which amplifier bands dodge the water peak is Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Rayleigh scattering from density fluctuations frozen into the glass, and Mie scattering from imperfections comparable to the wavelength, throw light out of the core; the Rayleigh term falls as 1/λ⁴ and sets the loss floor of modern fiber.
chapters.depth: Rayleigh scattering: light is scattered by microscopic density and composition fluctuations frozen in when the glass cools. The coefficient is α_R = (8π³/3λ⁴)·n⁸p²β_c·k·T_f, where λ is the wavelength, n the refractive index, p the photoelastic coefficient, β_c the isothermal compressibility, k Boltzmann's constant and T_f the fictive temperature at which the glass froze. The physics to remember is α_R ∝ 1/λ⁴. Typical values are about 1.9 dB/km at 850 nm, 0.34 dB/km at 1310 nm and 0.17 dB/km at 1550 nm; Rayleigh plus the infrared tail gives the familiar 0.2 dB/km floor. Mie scattering comes from imperfections of the order of the wavelength — rough core–cladding boundary, bubbles, unreacted particles, stress — with a weaker dependence, about 1/λ² in the worst case, and is kept below the Rayleigh term by good fabrication. Call these linear scattering: the loss does not depend on the optical power.

figure.aria: Two curves of scattering loss against wavelength: the Rayleigh curve falls steeply as the fourth power of wavelength, while the Mie curve stays small and nearly flat.

chapters.example: A fiber has a Rayleigh loss of 0.17 dB/km at 1550 nm and no measurable Mie term. (a) Estimate the Rayleigh loss at 1310 nm. (b) Estimate it at 850 nm. (c) The measured total at 850 nm is 2.5 dB/km; how much is left for other mechanisms? Answer: use α_R ∝ 1/λ⁴. (a) 0.17 × (1550/1310)⁴ = 0.17 × 1.96 = 0.33 dB/km. (b) 0.17 × (1550/850)⁴ = 0.17 × 11.06 = 1.9 dB/km. (c) 2.5 − 1.9 = 0.6 dB/km.
chapters.trap: Using λ⁴ instead of 1/λ⁴, which gets the direction wrong: loss falls as wavelength rises. Another trap is claiming Mie scattering dominates an ordinary telecom fiber.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for the attenuation coefficient, chapter 2 for where scattering sits in the loss picture.
chapters.leave: Power-dependent stimulated scattering is 2.9. Measuring the loss curve, for example with an OTDR, is Unit 5.

chapters.idea: When the fiber is bent, rays that strike the outer cladding beyond the critical angle escape, so bending adds loss, and that loss grows explosively as the bend radius falls below a critical value.
chapters.depth: Two kinds. Macro bending, also called macrocurvature loss: the whole fiber follows a curve of radius R and the guided field on the outside of the curve tunnels into the cladding and radiates. Loss per turn follows α = A e^(−BR), with A and B constants for that fiber, and stays small until R approaches the critical radius R_c ≈ (3n₁²λ)/(4π(n₁²−n₂²)^(3/2)), where n₁ is the core index, n₂ the cladding index and λ the free-space wavelength. Micro bending, also called microcurvature loss: small random wiggles caused by the coating, cabling, temperature or pressure couple core modes to cladding and radiation modes. Bending loss rises with wavelength, so a 1550 nm system suffers more than a 1310 nm one; bend-insensitive fiber adds a trench in the cladding. A few turns around a 10 mm mandrel is the usual shop-floor test.

figure.aria: A curve of bend loss per turn against bend radius, falling sharply as the radius grows, so small bends are far more costly.

chapters.example: A 1550 nm fiber has a measured bend-loss curve α = 8 e^(−0.6R) dB per turn, with R in mm. (a) Find the loss for one turn at R = 5 mm and at R = 10 mm. (b) Find the extra loss when a cable tray forces four turns at R = 5 mm. (c) Say why the same tray hurts less at 1310 nm. Answer: (a) at 5 mm, 8 × e^(−3) = 8 × 0.0498 = 0.40 dB; at 10 mm, 8 × e^(−6) = 8 × 0.00248 = 0.020 dB. (b) 4 × 0.40 = 1.6 dB. (c) Bending loss falls with wavelength, so at 1310 nm the same radius gives roughly half a dB less per turn.
chapters.trap: Assuming bending loss is worse at shorter wavelength, and forgetting that the figure is per turn, so it must be multiplied by the number of turns before it goes into the loss budget.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1, and Unit 1 for the critical angle and numerical aperture.
chapters.leave: Splice and connector misalignment losses are Unit 3. Cable design and mechanical reliability are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: In a multimode fiber different modes travel different path lengths, so one pulse arrives smeared over a range of times; the spread is proportional to length and index difference, and is far smaller in a graded-index fiber.
chapters.depth: Start from the two extreme rays. The axial ray covers length L in time L n₁/c. The steepest guided ray zig-zags and takes about L n₁/(c n₂). The difference for a step-index fiber is ΔT = (L n₁ Δ)/c, with Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁, L the length in metres and c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. For Δ = 0.01 this is roughly 50 ns per km, which is the classic multimode step-index number. A graded-index profile with a near-parabolic shape (profile parameter α ≈ 2) makes rays that swing far from the axis travel through lower-index glass, so they speed up and catch the axial ray; the best-case spread falls to ΔT = (L n₁ Δ²)/(2c), a factor of about Δ smaller. The bit rate is limited roughly by B·L ≤ 1/(2ΔT). Define the RMS width σ and the rule σ_total = √(σ_modal² + σ_chromatic²) for a multimode link, and say that a single-mode fiber has no intermodal term at all. Some syllabi call this modal dispersion or pulse dispersion.

figure.aria: Two straight lines of pulse spread against length: the step-index line climbs fifty times faster than the graded-index line.

chapters.example: A step-index multimode fiber has n₁ = 1.48, Δ = 0.01 and length L = 5 km. (a) Find the modal delay difference ΔT. (b) Estimate the maximum bit rate as 1/(2ΔT). (c) Repeat for a graded-index fiber with the optimum profile. Answer: (a) ΔT = (5000 × 1.48 / 3×10⁸) × 0.01 = 2.47×10⁻⁵ × 0.01 = 2.47×10⁻⁷ s ≈ 247 ns. (b) B = 1/(2 × 2.47×10⁻⁷) = 2.0 Mbit/s. (c) ΔT = 2.47×10⁻⁵ × (0.01)² / 2 = 1.23×10⁻⁹ s ≈ 1.2 ns, so B = 1/(2 × 1.23×10⁻⁹) ≈ 400 Mbit/s.
chapters.trap: Confusing Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁ with the plain difference n₁ − n₂, and losing the units so that the spread in ns cannot be compared with a bit period in ns.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for modes, numerical aperture and step versus graded profiles.
chapters.leave: Chromatic dispersion is 2.6. The total rise-time budget, which combines all the spread terms, is Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Because the source has a finite spectral width and the fiber's propagation constant depends on wavelength, different wavelengths arrive at different times; chromatic dispersion is the sum of a material and a waveguide part.
chapters.depth: Work in D in ps/(nm·km). The pulse spread is Δτ = D L Δλ, with L in km and Δλ the source spectral width in nm; if a laser is specified in GHz, convert with Δλ = (λ²/c)Δf. The total is D = D_m + D_w. Material dispersion comes from the wavelength dependence of the glass index, D_m = −(λ/c)(d²n/dλ²); it changes sign near 1300 nm and is positive and of order 20 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm. Waveguide dispersion comes from the way the mode's confinement, set by the V number, changes with wavelength; it is negative over the 1300–1600 nm range for a standard profile and is the part a designer tunes. Standard single-mode fiber has D = 0 near 1310 nm, D ≈ +17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm, and a slope near 0.09 ps/(nm²·km). Mention that the sign convention matters, and that a multimode link combines this term with 2.5 as a root-sum-square.

figure.aria: A tree showing chromatic dispersion as material dispersion plus waveguide dispersion, with the material zero near 1310 nm and the waveguide part tunable by profile design.

chapters.example: A 100 km single-mode link runs at 1550 nm with D = 17 ps/(nm·km). The laser linewidth is 0.1 nm. (a) Find the pulse spread Δτ. (b) Estimate the bit-rate limit as 1/(4Δτ). (c) Repeat (a) and (b) for a cheaper laser with a 2 nm linewidth. Answer: (a) Δτ = 17 × 100 × 0.1 = 170 ps. (b) B = 1/(4 × 170×10⁻¹²) ≈ 1.5 Gbit/s. (c) Δτ = 17 × 100 × 2 = 3400 ps = 3.4 ns, so B = 1/(4 × 3.4×10⁻⁹) ≈ 74 Mbit/s.
chapters.trap: Leaving out the source linewidth, or using a laser specified in GHz as if it were nm. Another trap is adding D_m and D_w without their signs.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 and Unit 1 for group velocity and the V number.
chapters.leave: Polarization mode dispersion is 2.7, dispersion-shifted and compensating fiber 2.8, and dispersion measurement and the rise-time budget are Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A real fiber is not perfectly circular, so the two polarization modes travel at slightly different speeds and their delay difference is random, growing as the square root of length.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Drawing and cabling leave the core slightly elliptical and under asymmetric stress, so the refractive index differs along two transverse axes: birefringence, n_x ≠ n_y. The two polarization modes then have different group delays. In a short, uniform fiber the differential group delay is Δτ = |β₁ₓ − β₁ᵧ| L, with β₁ the group delay per unit length. In a real cable the axes rotate at random along the length, so the delay adds in a random walk: the mean is ⟨Δτ⟩ = D_PMD √L, with D_PMD in ps/√km. The instantaneous DGD follows a Maxwellian distribution, so rare large values, near three times the mean, cause the outages. Modern fiber is about 0.05 to 0.2 ps/√km; older cable can exceed 1. Keep the mean DGD under roughly 10% of the bit period.

figure.aria: A curve of mean differential group delay against length that rises as the square root of length, not as a straight line.

chapters.example: A 400 km link uses fiber with a PMD coefficient of 0.1 ps/√km. (a) Find the mean DGD. (b) Compare it with the bit period at 10 Gbit/s and at 40 Gbit/s, taking 10% of the bit period as the limit. (c) Comment on the Maxwellian tail. Answer: (a) ⟨Δτ⟩ = 0.1 × √400 = 0.1 × 20 = 2 ps. (b) At 10 Gbit/s the bit period is 100 ps, limit 10 ps, so 2 ps is comfortable. At 40 Gbit/s the bit period is 25 ps, limit 2.5 ps, so the mean is already at the limit. (c) Values three times the mean, about 6 ps, exceed the limit and cause errors.
chapters.trap: Scaling DGD with L instead of √L. A second trap is treating PMD as a fixed number rather than a random quantity with a long tail.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for modes, and chapter 6 for the idea of group delay differences.
chapters.leave: Polarization controllers, polarizers and other components are Unit 6. PMD measurement is Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Instead of fighting dispersion, change the fiber: dispersion-shifted fiber moves the zero-dispersion wavelength to 1550 nm by redesigning the profile, and dispersion-compensating fiber adds a short length with large negative dispersion to cancel the link's positive dispersion.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Dispersion-shifted fiber (DSF) shrinks the core radius and raises Δ, which makes the waveguide term more negative at 1550 nm and moves the zero-dispersion point there. Non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber (NZDSF) keeps a small dispersion of about +2 to +6 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm so that four-wave mixing between WDM channels stays weak (Unit 6). Dispersion-compensating fiber (DCF) is a small-core, high-Δ fiber with strongly negative dispersion, of order −100 ps/(nm·km), wound on a spool; 10 to 20 km of it cancels 100 km of standard fiber. The design condition is Σ D_i L_i = 0 over the span. The cost is that DCF has higher loss, around 0.5 dB/km, and a small effective area, so it is more nonlinear. Slope mismatch leaves a residual dispersion at the band edges.

figure.aria: A chain from transmitter through 100 km of positive-dispersion fiber and 20 km of negative-dispersion compensating fiber to the receiver.

chapters.example: A 100 km span of standard single-mode fiber has D = +17 ps/(nm·km) and α = 0.2 dB/km. A compensating fiber has D = −85 ps/(nm·km) and α = 0.5 dB/km. (a) Find the DCF length for zero total dispersion. (b) Find the total loss of the span including the DCF. (c) Say what happens if only 15 km of DCF is available. Answer: (a) 17 × 100 = 85 × L, so L = 1700/85 = 20 km. (b) Loss = 0.2 × 100 + 0.5 × 20 = 20 + 10 = 30 dB. (c) Compensation is 17 × 100 − 85 × 15 = 1700 − 1275 = 425 ps/nm, a residual that must be checked against the bit-rate limit.
chapters.trap: Comparing dispersion coefficients without weighting them by length. Another trap is forgetting that the DCF adds loss and nonlinearity of its own.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6 for D, material and waveguide dispersion.
chapters.leave: Four-wave mixing and other WDM penalties are Unit 6, as is amplifier placement. The end-to-end budget is Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Above a threshold power, light in the fiber is pump-scattered into a wavelength-shifted wave, backward for Brillouin and forward for Raman, and that shifted wave steals power from the signal.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS): the signal beats with an acoustic wave and scatters backward a Stokes wave shifted by about 11 GHz at 1550 nm. The gain band is narrow, tens of MHz, so a narrow-line laser reaches threshold at only a few milliwatts. Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS): the signal scatters off molecular vibrations into a forward Stokes wave shifted by about 13 THz, with a gain band tens of THz wide; the threshold is in the hundreds of milliwatts. The threshold is P_th ≈ G A_eff/(g L_eff), where G ≈ 21 for Brillouin and G ≈ 16 for Raman, A_eff is the effective core area, g is the gain coefficient and L_eff = (1 − e^(−αL))/α is the effective length, about 1/α for a long span. Say what these do in service: SBS caps the power per WDM channel and reflects light toward the laser, SRS moves power from short-wavelength to long-wavelength channels. Name the uses, Brillouin sensors and Raman amplifiers, without teaching them.

figure.aria: A signal enters the fiber, a forward Stokes wave leaves it shifted up by about 13 THz from Raman scattering, and a dashed arrow returns a backward Stokes wave shifted down by about 11 GHz from Brillouin scattering.

chapters.example: A 1550 nm span has A_eff = 50 µm², gain coefficients g_B = 5×10⁻¹¹ m/W and g_R = 1×10⁻¹³ m/W, and an effective length of 20 km. (a) Find the Brillouin threshold. (b) Find the Raman threshold. (c) Comment for a WDM system with 4 mW per channel. Answer: (a) P_th = 21 × 50×10⁻¹² / (5×10⁻¹¹ × 2×10⁴) = 1.05×10⁻⁹ / 1×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.05×10⁻³ W, about 1 mW. (b) P_th = 16 × 50×10⁻¹² / (1×10⁻¹³ × 2×10⁴) = 8×10⁻¹⁰ / 2×10⁻⁹ = 0.4 W, about 400 mW. (c) At 4 mW per channel the Brillouin threshold is crossed, so the per-channel power is limited by SBS; the total power of all channels is still far below the Raman threshold.
chapters.trap: Using the physical length L where the formula needs L_eff, and swapping the two effects: Brillouin is backward with a GHz shift, Raman is forward with a THz shift.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for the attenuation coefficient, chapter 3 for the idea of scattering.
chapters.leave: Self-phase modulation, cross-phase modulation, four-wave mixing and solitons are Unit 6, along with Raman amplifiers and EDFAs.

links: absorption is the first term in the loss budget
absorption and scattering together set the loss floor
bending adds the third loss term
spontaneous scattering seeds the stimulated process
the attenuation coefficient fixes the effective length
both spread pulses and combine as a root-sum-square
chromatic and polarization dispersion both come from group delay differences
compensating fiber cancels the chromatic dispersion
